title: Do Reminders Work?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin examines whether verbal reminders actually improve student behavior, concluding that their effectiveness depends entirely on timing. He offers a simple rule of thumb: reminders given before misbehavior can occur are always good, while reminders given after misbehavior has already begun are always bad. Post-misbehavior reminders, he explains, substitute for a consequence and signal inconsistency, which erodes student trust and a teacher's authority over time. Pre-misbehavior reminders, by contrast, curb impulsivity by prompting self-awareness before students act. He also recommends giving reminders to the whole class rather than singling out individuals, since group reminders remove excuses without humiliating anyone. The piece ends by reiterating that once misbehavior begins, a consequence—not a reminder—is the only effective response.
points: Reminders given before misbehavior can occur are effective; reminders given after misbehavior has begun make things worse.
A post-misbehavior reminder substitutes for a consequence, signaling inconsistency that erodes student trust and teacher authority.
Pre-misbehavior reminders work by prompting self-awareness and making misbehavior a harder choice for students to make.
Reminders are best delivered to the entire class rather than to individual students, to avoid singling anyone out.
Once misbehavior has already started, the only effective response is a consequence, not another reminder.

The reason is that if you give a reminder when you first witness misbehavior, you’re doing so in lieu of giving a consequence , which by definition means you’re being inconsistent.
Although post-misbehavior reminders can help curb misbehavior in the moment—which is why so many teachers rely on them—the cost of doing so is exorbitantly high.
It gives them pause. It prompts self-awareness and causes them to focus on following your direction or fulfilling your objective.
It’s important to note that pre-misbehavior reminders are best given to the entire class rather than to just one student.
To sum up, reminders given to the entire class before misbehavior has a chance to develop are a big green light, and can be used as often as needed.
